subject: coralReef
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: coral reef with clownfish and anemones.
Style: Finding Nemo.
reasoning:
I'm picturing a Finding Nemo-style coral reef diorama with clownfish and anemones on a rocky seabed base, roughly a meter wide, and planning out the TypeScript module structure for building it.

I'll need a round plinth with sand/rock texture, plus a variety of coral types—branching staghorn, brain coral, tube coral, fan coral, and table coral—each built with different primitive approaches. For anemones, I'm thinking a base cylinder with rings of colored tentacles radiating outward using sweeps or spike patterns.

For tentacle count I need to budget carefully against the part limit—maybe 2 anemones with around 40 tentacles each using chunky low-side sweeps. The clownfish will be a trio (Marlin, Nemo, and a smaller one) built with skeletal chains for the spine, with lofted bodies painted orange and white with black outlines, fins and eyes attached, oriented head-forward along the z-axis.

I'm sketching a helper function to place each fish by applying rotation, scale, and translation to local coordinates, since paints keyed to body position stay unaffected by the transform. For rigging I need to settle on a single root joint for the whole scene that the individual fish joints can hang off of.

I'm also working out that scenery parts shouldn't automatically snap to the nearest fish joint, since that could make props move with swimming animations — so I'll explicitly assign a `bone` option on a helper function for static props to keep them anchored to a base joint instead.

For items like anemones, I'm worried that frame-based positioning without an explicit bone could cause them to inherit a nearby fish's joint. To avoid that risk, I'll skip the ring/frame helper for anemones and manually compute tentacle positions with sweeps bound explicitly to the root joint, using bezier curves to get a swaying motion.

For fish, I'll keep everything on explicit bones — sweeps built from a chain parented to the fish's root joint, with the eye as a separate part on a head joint. Joint and chain names will be prefixed per fish to stay unique, and I'm settling on a bright, saturated Finding Nemo-style palette, possibly with a cel-shaded toon look for the corals.

I'll mostly hand-write my own paints with warm-top/cool-bottom normal lighting rather than relying heavily on baked toon shading, since that keeps the atlas lean, but I'll still import the toon kit for select uses and consider a glow material for anemone tentacle tips.

Thinking through structure, I'll build each tentacle as two sweeps — a lower flat/paint section and a separate tip sweep that can glow in pale lilac — so I can isolate the glow effect rather than lighting the whole tentacle. I'll reserve glow for small accents like the glowing tip beads, and plan to scatter small reef extras like shells, starfish, and sea urchins around the clownfish and anemones.

Deciding to skip bubbles since they're not named in the brief, but keeping a modest starfish and a couple of urchins alongside the corals and anemones. Now I'm moving into layout planning, starting with the base disc at radius 0.55 and figuring out heights for how the coral and rock elements sit on top.

For the base, I'm shaping the lathe profile so it has a sandy, slightly domed top (around 0.56m wide) transitioning into a rockier skirt with strata-like layering on the sides, and I'll paint it by position -- sand tones with ripple mottling where y is higher, darker rock coloring lower down, using about 20 lathe segments for a smoother round shape.

I'm planning the overall reef composition now: a backdrop rock mass made from flattened icosahedra with greyish-purple mottling, then clusters of coral and sea life arranged around it -- staghorn coral on the left, brain and tube corals on the right, anemones with a clownfish front-center, a fan coral back-right, and a table coral on the left, all positioned relative to the viewer facing the front of the model.

Adding a second teal-lilac anemone at (0.28, G, 0.2) with radius 0.07, plus a smaller orange-yellow one at (-0.28, G, 0.28), and sketching out tentacle ring counts for density.

Then I'm planning the staghorn coral placement off to the side, working out positioning relative to viewer orientation before sketching the branching structure.

I'll write a recursive branch function: each limb is a tapered tube sweep with a slight curve, branching three ways across three levels for roughly 40 sweeps per cluster, with orange-to-pink gradient tips and flat-to-round caps.

For the child directions, I'm rotating the parent direction randomly by 25-40° using a cross-product perpendicular, with an upward bias, then coloring branches with a height-based gradient paint that mixes base coral and tip pink by smoothstep.

I'm checking paint resolution: with roughly 4 square meters of painted surface area, a 1024 texel sheet gives around 2.4mm texel density, which is fine, but I'll bump it up to 2048 for crisper fish stripes without overcomplicating the atlas.

For the brain coral, I'm squashing a sphere and painting it with a cell-based ridge pattern to create meandering grooves, using green-yellow tones with darker lines for the maze texture, and placing two instances at different sizes near the anemones. For the tube coral, I'm planning a cluster of tapered cylindrical shapes with dark hollow openings at the top to suggest tube-like structures.

Clustering seven purple-blue tube sponges of varying heights at the front left, built as lathe shapes with an outer wall and a dark disc or inner wall near the top to fake the hollow mouth, going for that Finding Nemo-style palette of purples, blues, and yellows.

Still defining paint logic...

For the fan coral, I'm thinking of using a thin extruded plate or a double-sided textured card with a sea-fan lattice pattern to get that lacy, holey look cheaply.

For table coral, I'll lathe a tapered stem into a wide dish shape, painting teal-to-lavender gradients with ring patterns.

For the sea urchin, I'm thinking through how to build spiky geometry by merging a sphere with many cone-shaped spikes scattered across the surface, avoiding lookAt/quaternion tricks and instead using a helper spike-building function per point.

For the starfish, I'm planning an extruded five-point star outline with bevel, placed flat on the sand, orange-red color, positioned slightly off-center near the front.

I'm skipping shells and instead sketching sea grass with card geometries scattered across the ground, using textured blade sprites with varied lean, bend, and size for natural sway.

For the fish, I'll keep it simple with three clownfish inspired by Finding Nemo: a larger female, a male like Marlin, and little Nemo featuring his signature smaller right pectoral fin as a nice character detail.

Working out proportions and coloring for each fish — orange bodies with black-outlined white stripes, nose-to-tail dimensions scaled per fish size, with Marlin getting three stripes across head, midbody, and tail base.

Now I'm designing the skeleton rig: placing spine points from tail base to head tip, then figuring out how to split them into two joint chains (front spine-to-head, back tail) branching from a shared root joint at the body center.

I'm planning a single body sweep spanning both chains with a catmull path from tail tip to nose, parameterizing t from 0 to 1 and defining a radius profile so the shape tapers appropriately along that length.

I'm sketching keyframe values for width and height at several points along t, with the thickest cross-section around 55% along the body and tapering toward a thin peduncle at the tail and a rounded nose, then writing a helper to interpolate those keys smoothly.

For the sweep frame, I'm confirming that with the path running along +Z, the normal axis stays vertical (up) and the binormal stays sideways, so my radius function's ry controls height and rx controls width consistently even after applying a yaw rotation to orient the fish.

Now I'm planning the coloring: base orange body with a lighter belly where the normal points downward and deeper orange on the back, then positioning Nemo's characteristic white stripes with thin black borders near the head, mid-body, and tail base using t-ranges along the body length.

Defining fin outlines and shapes...

I'm placing the tail fin bone on the tail tip joint at the end of the chain, matching the body sweep's structure where chains share a joint with the root core. Now I'm setting up the root joint parented to the reef.

Then I need the front chain's points for the spine and head joints, mapping the two spans to spine and head bone names, and figuring out how to assign roles to the chain versus the individual head joint.

I'll settle on a front chain named Spine/Head with the head joint as its second joint, then skin the body sweep across back/root/front bones, attaching dorsal and pec fins to their bones. For the mouth, I want a small clownfish-style separate upper and lower jaw—the lower jaw as a flattened orange ellipsoid with a lighter lip, plus an upper snout piece on the head.

Working out the exact proportions: a small jaw sphere scaled thin and positioned near the nose tip, with a dark flattened ellipsoid tucked above it to read as the mouth gap, keeping the geometry minimal while the body's rounded nose cap extends slightly past where the bulk of the body ends.

For the eyes, I want that classic Nemo look — white sclera with a dark pupil and glossy highlight — so I'm thinking of using a textured sphere or flat decal-like circle facing outward on the side of the head, making sure the texture's orientation lines up so the drawing faces along the X axis correctly.

I'm working out the eye geometry: a small cream-white sphere with a circular textured overlay, sized around 0.0125-0.017 radius, and figuring out its exact local position by checking the head's width at that point along the body's taper to make sure the eye sits proportionally right.

For the eye texture itself, I'm sketching an SVG design with a white base, thin black outline ring, a large black pupil, an amber-orange iris ring, and a couple of white highlight dots for that cartoonish chibi fish look.

I'm reusing this same eye texture for all fish since the circle geometry crops it into a disc nicely. For orientation, I'm aiming the eye circle outward and slightly forward-upward using a normalized direction vector so it reads naturally on both sides of the fish's head, keeping the highlight placement symmetrical enough that mirroring the texture for the opposite eye still looks right.

Now I'm working out the pectoral fins: attaching a rounded fan shape at each side of the body, angled backward and slightly outward for a natural resting pose, and computing the cross product of the fin's outline axes to get the correct thickness direction on each mirrored side.

For the fin outline itself, I'm sketching a small teardrop shape about 0.047 units long, with Nemo's smaller right fin scaled down to roughly 0.55x to match his distinctive asymmetry.

I need to figure out the sidedness convention: since +X is the fish's left in local coordinates, Nemo's lucky (smaller) right fin sits on the -X side, so I'll apply the 0.55 scale there. For the overall fish transform, I'm computing the yaw rotation about Y, applying it to local coordinates plus scale and position for points, and rotating direction vectors without scaling.

I'll build helper functions so all fish geometry is defined at unit scale and then multiplied by `sc` — one for points (rotate, scale, translate), one for plain scalar scaling of radii and outline coordinates, keeping the extrude code uncluttered since Three.js's extrude doesn't support scaling directly. Now I'm starting on the dorsal fin shape, beginning with its spiny front section.

Still shaping dorsal outline...

Writing dorsal fin paint logic...

Now I'm thinking through the ventral fins—small pelvic and anal fins placed underneath the body, extruded as compact outlines pointing backward and down, mirrored as a pair.

I'm reminding myself to stay disciplined given the target of 180-340 parts and 700-1100 lines, writing each piece carefully since I can't test-run it, and planning out the texture set: eye SVG, sea fan lattice, seagrass blade, and possibly coral polyp or anemone textures.

For more variety I'm considering kelp blades, feather-duster worm spirals in bright blue/yellow sitting on brain coral for that Finding Nemo charm, and soft coral polyp stars sprinkled across mounds, while skipping anything better handled as paint like caustics or starfish dots.

Settling on five core SVG textures—eye, fan lattice, grass blade, polyp star, and feather worm—since that feels like enough variety without overcomplicating the card system. Now I'm starting to set up imports for the Three.js builder utilities, geometry merging, and the various procedural helpers I'll need like noise, gradients, mottling, and SVG rendering.

Confirming the SDK's structure—everything exports from a single module, including meta info and constants like sand color palettes and surface height. I'm sketching out the reef's base paint function: sand mottled with ripple patterns on top, transitioning to layered rock strata on the sides based on surface normal and radius thresholds.

Still working out the lathe profile...

Items should embed slightly below the sand surface at G+0.01, with G set to 0.125. I'll ring rocks of varied sizes around the perimeter at radius 0.52 to act like a retaining wall, keeping the front ones smaller and covering the back more heavily for a natural diorama look.

For the rocks themselves, I'm using low-poly icosahedron geometry with flat shading, randomly scaled and rotated, then painted with a procedural rock shader blending dark and lit tones with noise, plus moss/algae coloring on upward-facing surfaces and pale coralline patches elsewhere.

Now moving to corals -- I'm writing a recursive branching function for staghorn coral that generates branch segments with randomized seeds and blends base-to-tip coloring along each branch.

Growing each branch segment as a curved sweep with a slight random bend, tapering radius from base to tip, and using round caps throughout so child branches blend smoothly into their parents. The random number generator is a seeded function returning successive pseudo-random values for consistent, reproducible branch variation.

For spawning child branches I'm working out directions by picking an azimuth around the parent's axis plus a tilt angle, then building an orthonormal basis perpendicular to the parent direction to rotate each child outward correctly.

I'm tapering length and radius by about 0.72 per branch generation, and sketching out branch counts per depth so a single tree ends up around 28 segments, aiming for a few differently-sized trees in varied colors like orange and pink.

I'm writing a gradient paint function that colors points along a branch from base to tip using a smoothstep on height, blended with noise speckling and normal-based shading for subtle texture.

Now I'm sketching the brain coral shape using a squashed low-poly sphere, with a paint function based on cellular/Voronoi noise to carve groove-like patterns mimicking the meandering ridges of real brain coral.

For painted decoration, flat shading feels fine for rocks but brain coral should stay smooth for readability. Now I'm planning a tube coral cluster using lathe shapes in vivid purple-blue and cyan tones, with seven tubes varying in height and radius, dark mouth openings, and about 10 segments each.

Next I'm sketching a table coral using a lathe outline — a thin stem rising then flaring outward into a wide, slightly concave cap, checking the point sequence doesn't self-intersect before setting segments to 14 with no smoothing.

For coloring, I want radial ridges computed from distance to center, shading from teal at the base to lilac at the rim with a white fringe, and maybe small polyps dotted on top. For the sea fans, I'll generate them programmatically as SVG with a recursive branching function radiating from a base point, drawing magenta-red strokes with cross-connections for texture. Writing SVG code...

Now I'm sketching the card setup for the fan shape with sizing and flow parameters, then moving on to designing a soft coral mound built from a rounded base plus small polyp cards scattered across it.

For Christmas tree worms on brain coral, I'm planning cards using a two-spiral feather cone texture, tufted and placed on hits filtered where the surface faces upward. Now starting on the anemone function next.

Shaping the anemone body...

I'm refining the tip bulb taper with five radius keys and splitting tentacle colors into bands so the tip reads a different hue than the shaft. Rather than merging dozens of bead geometries, I'll simplify by keeping tentacles thin with a tapered radius and no bulb, applying a gradient paint from base color to tip color along the tentacle's length instead of flat bands.

I'm giving Marlin a 20° yaw, Nemo a -35° yaw facing somewhat toward the viewer, and placing the smaller baby fish near a second anemone with a steep 70° yaw.

I'm settling the full layout now: anemone A (pink/purple classic) hosts Marlin and Nemo, anemone B (teal with lilac tips) hosts the baby clownfish, and a third anemone C (yellow-tan with orange tips) sits off to the side with no fish, just adding visual variety to the reef scene.

For the background, I'm placing a cluster of rock formations of varying sizes centered behind the anemones, and considering where to anchor a table coral on top of one of the taller rocks without it looking like it's floating awkwardly above the surface.

I'm placing elements asymmetrically: staghorn tree toward the left-back with a brain coral nearby, and table coral plus tube coral cluster on the right-back, checking that each position stays within the 0.5 base radius so nothing overhangs the edge.

For the front, I'm scattering anemones, sea grass, starfish, and sea urchins along the front edge within a safe 0.4 radius, then working out which angular range around the rim should get rocks—skipping the front arc so the view stays open, and placing rim rocks only through the back and side angles at steady intervals.

I'm staging tube clusters off to one side, checking they don't overlap too closely with the anemones, then placing a small soft coral mound tucked behind one of the anemones so it's partially hidden by the tentacles. Now I'm shifting focus to think through the camera setup.

I also want to double check the lathe outline arguments are typed correctly, making sure each point tuple matches the expected shape and the "sharp" corner markers are valid where used.

Checking that `flat: true` works for faceted normals on non-indexed geometry like the icosahedron, and that color params accept either a paint object or a string. Thinking through build order—creating the reef joint before the fish chains, since parts reference bones via `bone` and `at` placement in model space.

Now I'm defining the fish helper function, which takes an id, position, yaw, scale, and optional fin/stripe/mood parameters, then builds local rotation helpers for applying yaw around the Y axis before scaling and positioning each body part.

I'm sketching the joint hierarchy: a root joint at the body center with spine role, then a tail chain of joints following a Catmull-Rom curve through three points, named for two tail segments plus a tail fin tip.

Switching to a straight polyline for the front spine chain instead of a curve, since the points are collinear, naming the joints Spine1 and Head as spans off the root.

I realize I can also build the body as a single path from tail through root to nose using the back, root, and front bones together — a straight catmull/polyline through those three points, letting ring density follow radius changes along the tube.

For the stripe placement, I'm working out the t-values along the body where each white band sits: one just behind the eye near the head, one around the mid-body, and one near the tail, each defined as a center position with a halfwidth, with the orange head/snout region staying unstriped in front of the first band.

Writing bodyPaint function...

Fixing the import path, then working out the shading gradient toward the dorsal edge and sketching the tail fin outline as a series of coordinate points scaled to the model's unit size.

I'll settle on simple thresholds for the rim coloring and move to defining the pectoral fin outline, where the bone attaches rigidly to the body joint and the rim pattern follows the same white/black edge logic.
